title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired evaluation that compared a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime validator and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task). The preregistered primary test was a permutation‑based paired test; as a corroborating exact check we also computed an exact McNemar two‑sided test. Artifact‑backed results: complete pairs = 400; baseline successes = 400/400; guarded successes = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. No runtime repairs or rollbacks occurred (repair_applied = false across episodes). We interpret this null outcome as a ceiling effect produced by the preregistered shared_candidate design combined with the chosen generator+validator (every shared candidate satisfied the validator) rather than general evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary. We explicitly document construct‑validity consequences (the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 served as both runtime guard and as scorer), report the preregistered permutation result, cite the supporting analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg, analysis/results.json), and preserve an unresolved reporting limitation about aggregated difficulty counts (see Limitations and archived execution/task_manifest.jsonl).

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are rapidly being applied to NetOps problems that translate operator intent into device configurations and staged rollouts (canaries, progressive delivery, rollback). Prior prototypes and surveys highlight both promise for intent→configuration translation and a need for action‑aware benchmarks that exercise end‑to‑end staged rollout and auditability. Motivated by these gaps we preregistered and executed a paired experiment (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) that asked whether adding a deterministic runtime validator to an LLM agentic pipeline increases end‑to‑end safety (safe‑deploy rate) relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The design intentionally used shared_initial_generation (one shared LLM candidate per task) to isolate validator accept/block/repair decisions on identical generator outputs. Our contribution is an artifact‑backed, preregistered paired evaluation together with an evidence‑grounded failure analysis showing why the chosen design produced a null/ceiling outcome and guidance for benchmark hardening to expose verifier utility.
sections.related_work: Recent work documents intent→configuration translation and LLM‑assisted configuration generation in NetOps and related infrastructure domains (intent‑based NetOps, PreConfig, GraphSynth). Verifier‑augmented generate–validate–repair workflows have shown improvements in IaC and infrastructure settings (e.g., verifier‑guided IaC pipelines). Deterministic network verifiers and reachability tools can detect configuration errors offline. Agentic, tool‑augmented LLM pipelines and RAG/reasoning workflows are applied to AIOps/NetOps but introduce failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tool use) that motivate runtime guardrails. Surveyed literature repeatedly calls for action‑aware benchmarks that measure rollout, blocking, repair, rollback, and provenance; our experiment operationalizes a compact staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe these questions.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study preregistration (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with exactly N=400 deterministic tasks (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5), two conditions per task (baseline = LLM‑only, guarded = verifier‑augmented), shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task), and deterministic three‑replay consistency checks. The execution adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Model and runtime: declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json); runtime validator and post‑hoc scorer = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The adapter allowed up to one repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) but in this run no repairs were applied. Analysis plan: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; preregistered primary test = permutation‑based paired test (two‑sided, α=0.05). The preregistration also specified secondary bootstrap CIs for descriptive outcomes and a single primary hypothesis (no multiplicity across the primary test). Execution and provenance: all runtime calls, raw responses, validator traces, deterministic replays, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts were archived (execution/* and analysis/*). Deterministic three‑replay checks were applied; no task met exclusion criteria.

sections.discussion: Why a null/ceiling outcome occurred: two preregistered design choices produced a practical ceiling that made the primary estimand untestable in this run. First, shared_initial_generation semantics provided identical generator outputs for baseline and guarded conditions by design; this isolates validator behavior but eliminates generation variance as a pathway for the guarded adapter to change outcomes. Second, the particular generator+validator pairing produced universally valid shared candidates under the deterministic validator: every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, so the guard had no opportunity to block or request a repair. Construct validity consequence: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation was used both as the guarded runtime acceptor/blocker and as the post‑hoc scorer that determined safe‑deploy outcomes (see execution/scoring/* artifacts and validator_trace fields). This conflation biases concordance and limits inference to validator acceptance on identical candidates rather than to independent closed‑loop generator+guard dynamics. Statistical interpretation: the preregistered permutation test (primary) returned p = 1.0 and the exact McNemar two‑sided check agreed (p = 1.0); bootstrap CIs are degenerate at 0.0 due to identical paired outcomes. Implications for future designs: to reveal runtime verifier utility, experiments should (a) allow independent per‑condition generation (remove shared_initial_generation), (b) introduce targeted fault/adversarial injections or generator perturbations that produce nontrivial invalid candidates, or (c) evaluate heterogeneous generators/validators so acceptance rates differ. The archived artifacts (execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/responses/*, analysis/*) can be used as starting inputs for such hardened experiments.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator configuration, every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic validator; both conditions achieved 100% safe‑deploy on N=400 pairs and the preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0. This null/ceiling outcome stems from design choices (shared candidate semantics and using the same deterministic validator as guard and scorer) that removed opportunities for the guard to alter deployments. Therefore the results do not indicate that runtime verification is unnecessary in general. We release the preregistration, execution artifacts, validator traces, and analysis outputs so readers can reproduce the run and use the artifacts to design hardened evaluations that exercise blocking and repair behaviors. Note: an aggregated per‑task difficulty histogram was not summarized in the top‑level manuscript artifacts; the full per‑task difficulty labels are available in execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the artifact bundle (preserved reporting limitation; see Limitations).

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory): This study was produced under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track autonomy boundary. The autonomous run used the declared model version gpt-5-mini (see execution/model_configuration.json). The orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (single shared initial candidate per task; independent_condition_generation = false). The exact immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Topic constraints (selected pre‑lock by the Research Director) limited the work to generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focused on reliability/safety of intent→configuration generation. The experimental framework and preregistration are archived as cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 and were frozen before execution (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest). Tools and capabilities permitted: hosted model API calls (provider record in execution/model_configuration.json), deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for configuration scoring and guarding, deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 for task generation, and paired_binary_analysis_v1 for confirmatory analysis. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically scored candidates and acted as an acceptor/blocker under the preregistered adapter policy; the execution contract allowed up to one repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) but no repairs were applied in any episode (artifact field repair_applied = false across episodes). The study used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) as a preregistered design choice; this explicitly reduces generation variance across conditions and therefore measures validator acceptance/repair behavior on identical candidates. The preregistered analysis plan specified a permutation‑based paired test for the primary estimand; the archived confirmatory analysis reports the permutation p = 1.0 and an exact McNemar two‑sided corroborating check p = 1.0; paired bootstrap CIs were computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples. All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived with the execution manifest (execution/* and analysis/* in the artifact bundle). Autonomous literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting occurred post‑lock under the autonomy constraints of the master prompt; no human manually edited the technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred (permitted by the track) but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as final empirical evidence unless reproduced in the post‑lock run.
limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: tasks were synthetic and, under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and chosen generator+validator, produced universally valid shared candidates so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and as the post‑hoc scorer (see execution/scoring/* artifacts); this conflation biases concordance and limits inference to validator acceptance on identical candidates rather than independent closed‑loop generator+guard dynamics.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance across conditions and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production runtime uncertainties, telemetry noise, adversarial intent, or operator workflows; external validity to live networks is limited.
Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open.

Aggregated difficulty reporting gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the representative sample in manuscript artifacts (six tasks) showed 1× medium, 2× hard, 3× very_hard; a complete aggregated histogram by difficulty was not summarized in the top‑level manuscript artifacts and therefore remains a reporting limitation preserved here—readers can derive the full aggregation from execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the artifact bundle.
